Besides moving lines for the removed dependencies, the diff drops azblob v1.3.2 and go-replayers/grpcreplay and httpreplay entries from go.work.sum. These entries are unrelated to the go-duck removal. The removal could break workspace builds for modules that still need those checksums, and it suggests a `go work sync` or tidy was run with side effects that were not intended.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrent BuildIndex for the same key is no longer serialized

The whole-function lock is removed, but nothing replaces it as per-key protection. `getOrCreateIndex` does an unlocked get-then-build, so two concurrent callers for the same key (for example a search request and a watch event) can both build. For file-backed indexes, `bleve.New(dir)` then fails because the path already exists. For memory indexes, one index silently overwrites the other in the cache, leaving the first as a leaked orphan whose metrics were already incremented. Finer-grained locking should be per key (singleflight or a per-key mutex), not only around the map write.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the cache map without holding cacheMu

`BuildIndex` now takes `cacheMu` only around the map write, and `TotalDocs` reads `b.cache` with no lock. The PR adds a call to `s.search.TotalDocs()` in `searchSupport.init`, right after the goroutine that handles watch events has been started. That goroutine can call `getOrCreateIndex` and then `BuildIndex`, which writes the map concurrently with the read. This is a concurrent map read/write, which Go can turn into a fatal panic. `TotalDocs` should take `cacheMu.RLock()`.

false_positives.candidate:
Data races in the init worker goroutines

Inside the errgroup closure, `totalBatchesIndexed++` and the assignment `_, _, err = s.build(...)` write shared variables from several goroutines without synchronization. `err` is the outer variable declared by `GetResourceStats`. This was already racy, but init now always runs at startup with `initWorkers` goroutines. The race can corrupt the counter and also lose or mix errors. Use an atomic counter and a local `err` inside the closure.

Postgres integration test skipped, possibly masking a regression from eager init

The test is skipped for postgres with a note that it works locally but not in Drone. This PR changes startup so the resource server initializes eagerly, and the test is exactly the one that starts the storage-server target, which is the path affected. Disabling it removes the only coverage for that path on postgres, and the cause is not investigated. Linking a tracking issue, or confirming the failure is unrelated to this change, would make the skip safer.

Removing per-request Init checks drops the stopped/failed-init guard

Every RPC used to call `s.Init(ctx)` and return `s.initErr`. `Stop()` sets `initErr` to "service is stopping" or "service is stopped", so requests arriving after shutdown began were rejected. With the checks gone, nothing reads `initErr` after construction. Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch and Search now run against a stopped server: the lifecycle hooks have stopped, the DB may be closing and the context is cancelled. Callers get arbitrary backend errors or hangs instead of a clear error. The reviewer's question about lazy init is partly answered here: the only post-start use of that state is lost. Keep a cheap state check (for example an atomic stopped flag) in the request paths.

Server construction now blocks on a full index build and fails hard on any error

`NewResourceServer` now runs `s.Init(ctx)` synchronously. That runs the lifecycle hooks, builds the search index for every namespace and resource above the size threshold, and starts the watcher. Constructing the server, and therefore module startup and wire/DI, blocks for the entire index build. Any error, such as one namespace failing to index or a transient DB failure, makes construction return an error. Before, such an error was cached and returned per request. For large installs, startup latency and liveness probes need consideration, and a single bad index should probably not take the whole server down.

Trace context is still dropped in BuildIndex and several SQL backend methods

The PR claims to fix trace propagation, but `BuildIndex` still does `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` and discards the derived context. In `sql/backend.go`, `WriteEvent`, `ReadResource` and `ListIterator` have the same problem. Spans created below these functions therefore do not become children of the span started here. The fix was applied to `GetResourceStats`, `init` and `build`, but not to these.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup registered with literal "alias" instead of the created alias, leaking IDPs

`getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` targets an IDP literally named "alias", not the IDPs created in the loop (`idp-alias-N`). The same bug is at line 425 for `idp-alias-20`. None of the 21 IDPs created by `testCacheIDPForLogin` are cleaned up, and the cleanup itself may fail with 404. Leftover login IDPs can pollute other tests in the same realm, such as the exact counts asserted in this test or `OrganizationCacheTest` reruns. The cleanup should use the actual alias.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Update invalidation decision uses the org-aware wrapped model, which can skip a needed login-cache invalidation

`update()` takes the original IDP from `getById()`, which returns the org-aware wrapper. For an IDP linked to an org, the wrapper's `isEnabled()` also requires the org and the organization feature to be enabled. `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate` then calls `getLoginPredicate().test(original)`, so an enabled IDP in a disabled org looks 'not a login IDP'. The cached login lists are built from the stored attributes (JPA query on `enabled=true` etc.) and still contain that IDP. If the IDP is then updated so that the new state is also 'not login' (for example `hideOnLogin=true`), the early return skips invalidation. The stale entry stays in the cache, and when the org is re-enabled the IDP is wrongly shown on the login page. The comparison should use the unwrapped stored model, for example from `idpDelegate.getById`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead duplicate encoder calls in concatenatedRSToASN1DER

`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and the same for `sBigInteger` encode the values and discard the result. They have no effect, and the values are encoded again in the `writeDerSeq` call below. Remove them. The method also does not validate that `signature` has at least `signLength` bytes. A short, attacker-supplied JWS signature produces an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` instead of an `IOException`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract `order()` method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

`order()` is added as an abstract interface method. Any external or custom `CryptoProvider` implementation, such as third-party or testsuite providers, will no longer compile. Already-compiled ones will fail with `AbstractMethodError` inside the `sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order))` call in `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider`. A `default int order() { return 0; }` would keep source and binary compatibility.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
Conflicting crypto providers are now silently picked instead of failing

The old check threw "Multiple crypto providers loaded" when more than one provider was on the classpath. It is removed and replaced by sorting on `order()`. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200. A misconfigured classpath, such as default plus FIPS or default plus Elytron, now picks one by `ServiceLoader` order, which depends on classpath order. The rest are only mentioned at debug level. Before, this was a hard failure; now a FIPS deployment could silently run on the non-FIPS provider. Equal-order conflicts should still throw, or at least be logged at warn. Only the authz-client fallback (order 100) should be allowed to lose to another provider.

Indefinite or oversized length leads to unchecked exceptions or unbounded allocation

`readLength()` returns -1 for the indefinite-length form (0x80). `readInteger()` then calls `read(length)` with -1, which throws `NegativeArraySizeException` instead of `IOException`. The `length >= limit` bounds check applies only to the long form. Short-form lengths are bounded by 127, but `read(int)` does not otherwise validate against the remaining input. Malformed DER input should be rejected with `IOException`. Reject negative lengths in `readInteger`/`readNext` and check the length against `is.available()`.

Round-trip test never validates the DER encoder independently

The test only checks that decode(encode(decode(x))) equals decode(x). It never verifies that the DER produced by `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` is accepted by a real JDK `Signature.verify`, and it never covers edge cases. Those edge cases include r/s with the high bit set, r/s shorter than the curve length (leading zeros), and malformed or indefinite-length input. A round trip with a symmetric bug would still pass. Compare the encoder output against the original JDK-produced DER and verify the signature with it.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No cleanup of Clients-type resources when a client is deleted under V2

The listener is now gated on `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ`, so under V2 `ClientRemovedEvent` does nothing. A client's per-client resource and any permissions referencing it remain in the admin-permissions resource server after the client is deleted. The orphaned resource is named by the old client id. There is no V2 cleanup path. Also, the gate changes existing V1 behaviour, because the listener previously ran whenever the V1 listener was registered, regardless of the feature flag.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission may return the type resource name and evaluates every resource

`findByType(server, "Clients", ...)` also matches the all-clients type resource, whose name is the literal "Clients" and not a client id. That string can end up in the returned set of client ids. Each resource is also evaluated separately through `root.evaluatePermission`, so the cost grows with the number of clients that have per-client resources. The type resource should be skipped, and the evaluation cost noted or reduced.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Possible NPE when the all-clients resource cannot be resolved

When no per-client resource exists, `getResourceTypeResource(...)` is used as the fallback and passed straight to `findByResource(server, resource)`. That method returns null if the schema is not supported for the server, if admin permissions are disabled for the realm, or if the 'Clients' resource is missing. The result is a NullPointerException, which surfaces as a 500 instead of a plain 'no permission' false. A null check should return false.

true_positives.golden_comment: Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code and unused imports

`getEvaluationContext` is never called, so `ClientModelIdentity`, `DefaultEvaluationContext`, `EvaluationContext`, `AccessToken` and the helper itself are dead. `logger`, the static import `TOKEN_EXCHANGE` and the `Scope` import are also unused. This is copy-paste residue and should be removed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
JUnit 4 fail() used in a JUnit 5 test

`org.junit.Assert.fail` is imported while the rest of the class and sibling tests use `org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions`. Mixing in the JUnit 4 API depends on a transitive dependency and is inconsistent.

Tests mutate shared client state without restoring it

`testManageOnlyOneClient` renames `myclient` and removes a default client scope, then re-adds it only as an optional scope. `testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient` creates client roles. `onAfter` removes only permissions, so this state leaks into other tests on the same realm. `testConfigureOnlyOneClient` indexes `getDefaultClientScopes().get(0)`, so results can depend on test order.

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Existing recreate-upgrade exit code silently changed from 4 to 3

RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE moves from 4 to 3 and 4 is reused for FEATURE_DISABLED. Any script or pipeline that already treats exit code 4 as "recreate required" will now read 4 as "feature disabled" and 3 as recreate. The documented meaning of the codes changes in place. The guide also still describes this tool as an evolving preview, but anything that already consumed the old code is broken without notice. Consumers inside the repo, such as the Operator code that runs the check, must be audited and updated. This diff does not touch any.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

false_positives.candidate:
Appended --features flag is placed after user parameters in every generated example

The macro appends `--features=rolling-updates` after `${parameters}` in all generated update-compatibility examples. The guide text then tells users to supply the same options as for `start`, but the example hides the fact that the feature is required. Only the CAUTION block mentions it. The `--features` value also replaces rather than adds to the user's feature list when they already pass `--features`, and the docs do not warn about this.

Also, `--features=rolling-updates` is a build-time option. When the server is run with `--optimized` (a mixin is present on these commands), a feature that was not enabled at build time is not picked up. The same applies to the identical check in UpdateCompatibilityMetadata. The only behaviour tested is the non-optimized dist case.

testFeatureNotEnabled only asserts the error message for the `metadata` subcommand. It does not assert exit code 4, which is the new contract that scripts rely on and is documented. It also never exercises `check` with the feature disabled. A regression in the `check` path, or in the exit code, would go unnoticed.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() on all-groups is granted by the VIEW scope

`canManage()` in V2 calls `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`. It returns true when the admin has only the `view` scope on the all-groups resource. `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup` calls `requireManage()`, so an admin with view-only access to all groups could create top-level groups. The Javadoc in `GroupPermissionEvaluator` documents the same wrong behaviour ("VIEW or MANAGE groups"). It should check only `MANAGE`. true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission mixes up the resource id and the group id

The callback in `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission` calls `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)` and then adds `groupResource.getId()` to the result. In `hasPermission`, the first argument is used as a name: `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`. The returned set contains resource ids rather than group ids, yet callers (`UsersResource` and `BruteForceUsersResource`) use it to filter users by group membership and for the users count. switch on a null resourceType throws NPE

false_positives.candidate:
Strategy close() shuts down the factory-shared queue pool; the next rebalance silently drops and commits messages

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`, `terminate()` and `join()` call `queue_pool.shutdown()`. That pool is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and reused by every strategy from `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker`. Arroyo closes the strategy and calls `create_with_partitions` again on every partition rebalance. After the first rebalance the new strategy therefore gets a pool whose workers have exited and whose queues are shut down. `queue.put` then raises `queue.ShutDown`. `submit()` catches that with its generic `except Exception`, calls `add_offset` and `complete_offset`, and the offset becomes committable. The result is that every message after a rebalance is dropped and its offset committed, which is data loss. The pool should be created per strategy, or the strategy should not own the shared pool's lifecycle. The `OffsetTracker` is also shared across rebalances, so stale offsets and `last_committed` for revoked partitions persist.

Any failure while enqueuing is treated as 'processed' and the offset is committed

The broad `except Exception` in `submit()` logs the error, then registers and immediately completes the offset. That includes failures of `queue_pool.submit` (for example `queue.ShutDown`) and of `grouping_fn`. The offset becomes committable and the message is permanently skipped. Only decode failures (result is None) should be skipped this way. Infrastructure errors should be raised or retried so the message is not lost.

Claimed backpressure does not exist; queues and offset tracker are unbounded

The docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up'. The queues are `queue.Queue()` with no maxsize, `submit()` never blocks, and `poll()` never raises `MessageRejected`. If one queue is slow, which is the scenario this PR targets, the consumer keeps reading from Kafka. Messages accumulate in memory without bound. `all_offsets` grows with them, and so does the per-commit `range()` scan. The consumer can run out of memory, and the offset stuck at the slow item can never advance. Use bounded queues and reject or block when full.

Kafka commit callback is invoked from a background thread

`commit_function` (arroyo's `commit`) is called from `_commit_loop`, a separate daemon thread, while the StreamProcessor main thread is polling and managing the consumer. Arroyo's commit callback and the Kafka consumer state are designed to be used from the processing thread. Calling them concurrently risks races and corrupted offset state. The commit is also not tied to partition ownership, so offsets can be committed for partitions already revoked during a rebalance. Commits should be issued from `poll()`/`submit()` in the main thread.

Non-contiguous Kafka offsets stall commits forever

Commit advancement requires every integer offset in the range to be present in `all_offsets`. Offsets that are never delivered to the strategy (transaction control markers, compacted or skipped offsets) look like a permanent gap. Commits for that partition then stall indefinitely and `all_offsets` and `outstanding` grow without bound. The gap test encodes this as intended behaviour. A tracker keyed on submitted offsets (commit up to the lowest outstanding offset minus one) would avoid it.

Distribution test depends on randomized string hashing

`test_different_groups_distributed` asserts that 20 group keys cover all 3 queues. The queue index comes from `hash(str)`, which is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED). There is a small but non-zero chance (about 0.1%) that a queue is missed, so the test can fail occasionally.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract `order()` method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

`order()` is added as an abstract interface method. Any external or custom `CryptoProvider` implementation, such as third-party or testsuite providers, will no longer compile. Already-compiled ones will fail with `AbstractMethodError` inside the `sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order))` call in `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider`. A `default int order() { return 0; }` would keep source and binary compatibility.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward-compatibility issue: adding an abstract order() method to CryptoProvider breaks existing implementations. The candidate adds specific source and runtime consequences and a compatible default-method solution.

false_positives.candidate:
Conflicting crypto providers are now silently picked instead of failing

The old check threw "Multiple crypto providers loaded" when more than one provider was on the classpath. It is removed and replaced by sorting on `order()`. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200. A misconfigured classpath, such as default plus FIPS or default plus Elytron, now picks one by `ServiceLoader` order, which depends on classpath order. The rest are only mentioned at debug level. Before, this was a hard failure; now a FIPS deployment could silently run on the non-FIPS provider. Equal-order conflicts should still throw, or at least be logged at warn. Only the authz-client fallback (order 100) should be allowed to lose to another provider.

Indefinite or oversized length leads to unchecked exceptions or unbounded allocation

`readLength()` returns -1 for the indefinite-length form (0x80). `readInteger()` then calls `read(length)` with -1, which throws `NegativeArraySizeException` instead of `IOException`. The `length >= limit` bounds check applies only to the long form. Short-form lengths are bounded by 127, but `read(int)` does not otherwise validate against the remaining input. Malformed DER input should be rejected with `IOException`. Reject negative lengths in `readInteger`/`readNext` and check the length against `is.available()`.

Round-trip test never validates the DER encoder independently

The test only checks that decode(encode(decode(x))) equals decode(x). It never verifies that the DER produced by `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` is accepted by a real JDK `Signature.verify`, and it never covers edge cases. Those edge cases include r/s with the high bit set, r/s shorter than the curve length (leading zeros), and malformed or indefinite-length input. A round trip with a symmetric bug would still pass. Compare the encoder output against the original JDK-produced DER and verify the signature with it.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hung flusher process is never killed because the isinstance check never matches SpawnProcess

When a flusher is declared hung (`cause == "hang"`), it is not killed and a replacement is started for the same shards. Two flushers then run on the same shards and the old one leaks. Repeated restarts accumulate orphaned processes, and duplicate segments can be flushed. The same wrong check in `join()` (line 346) means `terminate()` is never called either. Check against `threading.Thread` instead, or use `hasattr(process, 'kill')`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: spawn-context processes are SpawnProcess instances that do not satisfy the multiprocessing.Process isinstance check on POSIX, so hung flusher processes are not killed.

false_positives.candidate:

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`, `terminate()` and `join()` call `queue_pool.shutdown()`. That pool is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and reused by every strategy from `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker`. Arroyo closes the strategy and calls `create_with_partitions` again on every partition rebalance. After the first rebalance the new strategy therefore gets a pool whose workers have exited and whose queues are shut down. `queue.put` then raises `queue.ShutDown`. `submit()` catches that with its generic `except Exception`, calls `add_offset` and `complete_offset`, and the offset becomes committable. The result is that every message after a rebalance is dropped and its offset committed, which is data loss. The pool should be created per strategy, or the strategy should not own the shared pool's lifecycle. The `OffsetTracker` is also shared across rebalances, so stale offsets and `last_committed` for revoked partitions persist.

Any failure while enqueuing is treated as 'processed' and the offset is committed

The broad `except Exception` in `submit()` logs the error, then registers and immediately completes the offset. That includes failures of `queue_pool.submit` (for example `queue.ShutDown`) and of `grouping_fn`. The offset becomes committable and the message is permanently skipped. Only decode failures (result is None) should be skipped this way. Infrastructure errors should be raised or retried so the message is not lost.

Claimed backpressure does not exist; queues and offset tracker are unbounded

The docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up'. The queues are `queue.Queue()` with no maxsize, `submit()` never blocks, and `poll()` never raises `MessageRejected`. If one queue is slow, which is the scenario this PR targets, the consumer keeps reading from Kafka. Messages accumulate in memory without bound. `all_offsets` grows with them, and so does the per-commit `range()` scan. The consumer can run out of memory, and the offset stuck at the slow item can never advance. Use bounded queues and reject or block when full.

Kafka commit callback is invoked from a background thread

`commit_function` (arroyo's `commit`) is called from `_commit_loop`, a separate daemon thread, while the StreamProcessor main thread is polling and managing the consumer. Arroyo's commit callback and the Kafka consumer state are designed to be used from the processing thread. Calling them concurrently risks races and corrupted offset state. The commit is also not tied to partition ownership, so offsets can be committed for partitions already revoked during a rebalance. Commits should be issued from `poll()`/`submit()` in the main thread.

Non-contiguous Kafka offsets stall commits forever

Commit advancement requires every integer offset in the range to be present in `all_offsets`. Offsets that are never delivered to the strategy (transaction control markers, compacted or skipped offsets) look like a permanent gap. Commits for that partition then stall indefinitely and `all_offsets` and `outstanding` grow without bound. The gap test encodes this as intended behaviour. A tracker keyed on submitted offsets (commit up to the lowest outstanding offset minus one) would avoid it.

Distribution test depends on randomized string hashing

`test_different_groups_distributed` asserts that 20 group keys cover all 3 queues. The queue index comes from `hash(str)`, which is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED). There is a small but non-zero chance (about 0.1%) that a queue is missed, so the test can fail occasionally.

Denial cache can keep denying a user right after permissions are granted or a resource is created

A denial is cached for 30s under (ns, user, action, name, folder), and nothing invalidates it. This includes name-less checks such as folders:create, where name and parent are empty. If a check for a resource runs before the user's permission exists (an existence probe before creation, or a permission granted moments later), the user is denied for up to 30s even after the DB is correct. That partly defeats the PR goal that creators can immediately access what they just created.

Requery on cache miss refreshes permissions but not the folder tree

On a cached-permission denial the code re-fetches permissions from the DB, but checkPermission then calls buildFolderTree, which uses the folder cache with a 30s TTL. A user who creates a new folder, or a dashboard in a newly created folder, can still be denied inherited access until the folder cache expires. This is because the new folder is not in the cached tree, so the requery does not fully fix the new-folder case.

The 'from cache' test case was deleted, so cacheHit is always false and the cacheHit branches (the s.permCache.Set and the `store.calls == 1` assertion) are dead code. The remaining case named 'should return error if store fails' expects no error. Together these make the test misleading, and the change that moved the cache lookup out of getUserPermissions has no direct test.

This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

After the read-lock fast path misses, every concurrent caller that saw a nil cache serializes on `Lock()` and then re-reads the manifest file (and possibly makes an HTTP call) one by one. There is no second check of `entryPointAssetsCache` under the write lock. At startup, or after a failed load, N concurrent requests do N redundant loads while the others block. In Dev mode every call takes the exclusive lock and does file I/O under it, which serializes all requests that need web assets. Add a double-checked `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` after `Lock()`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache overwritten with nil on error, and err may be masked

`entryPointAssetsCache = result` runs even when `err != nil`, so a transient read failure (or a Dev-mode reload failure) replaces a previously valid cache with nil. Callers then get `(nil, err)`. This is existing behavior, but the lock now makes it a deliberate write path. Only assign the cache on success. Also, if the `cdn` branch fails, `err` is set and `result` is nil, and the file fallback then reassigns `err`, which is fine. A partial result is never cached, though, so the guard should be explicit.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same unconditional cache assignment on fetch failure, where a nil result overwrites a previously valid cache entry. Its additional discussion of error masking does not change this match.

Otherwise it uses placeholders, and those are limited only by the batch size, so this part is fine. However, the 999 limit is the pre-3.32 default, so newer SQLite builds pay for building a huge string for no reason. A real concern: annotation_tag may have no `id` column in some schemas (the original query also used `id`), so the behaviour is the same as before. true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. false_positives.candidate:
Strategy close() shuts down the factory-shared queue pool; the next rebalance silently drops and commits messages

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`, `terminate()` and `join()` call `queue_pool.shutdown()`. That pool is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and reused by every strategy from `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker`. Arroyo closes the strategy and calls `create_with_partitions` again on every partition rebalance. After the first rebalance the new strategy therefore gets a pool whose workers have exited and whose queues are shut down. `queue.put` then raises `queue.ShutDown`. `submit()` catches that with its generic `except Exception`, calls `add_offset` and `complete_offset`, and the offset becomes committable. The result is that every message after a rebalance is dropped and its offset committed, which is data loss. The pool should be created per strategy, or the strategy should not own the shared pool's lifecycle. The `OffsetTracker` is also shared across rebalances, so stale offsets and `last_committed` for revoked partitions persist.

Any failure while enqueuing is treated as 'processed' and the offset is committed

The broad `except Exception` in `submit()` logs the error, then registers and immediately completes the offset. That includes failures of `queue_pool.submit` (for example `queue.ShutDown`) and of `grouping_fn`. The offset becomes committable and the message is permanently skipped. Only decode failures (result is None) should be skipped this way. Infrastructure errors should be raised or retried so the message is not lost.

Claimed backpressure does not exist; queues and offset tracker are unbounded

The docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up'. The queues are `queue.Queue()` with no maxsize, `submit()` never blocks, and `poll()` never raises `MessageRejected`. If one queue is slow, which is the scenario this PR targets, the consumer keeps reading from Kafka. Messages accumulate in memory without bound. `all_offsets` grows with them, and so does the per-commit `range()` scan. The consumer can run out of memory, and the offset stuck at the slow item can never advance. Use bounded queues and reject or block when full.

Kafka commit callback is invoked from a background thread

`commit_function` (arroyo's `commit`) is called from `_commit_loop`, a separate daemon thread, while the StreamProcessor main thread is polling and managing the consumer. Arroyo's commit callback and the Kafka consumer state are designed to be used from the processing thread. Calling them concurrently risks races and corrupted offset state. The commit is also not tied to partition ownership, so offsets can be committed for partitions already revoked during a rebalance. Commits should be issued from `poll()`/`submit()` in the main thread.

Non-contiguous Kafka offsets stall commits forever

Commit advancement requires every integer offset in the range to be present in `all_offsets`. Offsets that are never delivered to the strategy (transaction control markers, compacted or skipped offsets) look like a permanent gap. Commits for that partition then stall indefinitely and `all_offsets` and `outstanding` grow without bound. The gap test encodes this as intended behaviour. A tracker keyed on submitted offsets (commit up to the lowest outstanding offset minus one) would avoid it.

Distribution test depends on randomized string hashing

`test_different_groups_distributed` asserts that 20 group keys cover all 3 queues. The queue index comes from `hash(str)`, which is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED). There is a small but non-zero chance (about 0.1%) that a queue is missed, so the test can fail occasionally.

`record.match_count += 1; record.save` loads the value into Ruby, increments it, and writes it back. Concurrent signups with the same blocked email will lose updates. Use `update_all` or `increment_counter` with an atomic SQL increment instead.

Separately, `value` can be nil. `email_in_restriction_setting?` would then compute `nil =~ regexp`, which returns nil, so a whitelist would add an error to a nil value. This is harmless when presence already fails, but the code is fragile.

The file has no trailing newline, as the diff itself shows with `\ No newline at end of file`.

Retrying then fails with 'emails_must_be_unique_valid' because the guests already exist. There is no transaction or compensation. The `catch` around the email send only does `console.log` and discards the error.

Credentials and EventManager use the acting user, not the organizer

`getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and `new EventManager({...user})` use the logged-in user's credentials. When an attendee or team admin adds guests, the calendar event owned by the organizer is updated with the wrong user's credentials. The update can fail or silently do nothing. The booking's organizer credentials (already included in the query) should be used.

New guests take the organizer's locale and timezone

Guests are created with the organizer's `timeZone` and `locale`, so guest emails and times are rendered in the organizer's locale and timezone rather than the guest's. New guests also have an empty name.

`const message = `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`` is always a non-empty string, so `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` never triggers. Users see messages like 'BAD_REQUEST: emails_must_be_unique_valid' prefixed with a raw error code. Also, `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` is recreated on every render inside the component.

The 'additional_guests' action is added unconditionally to `editBookingActions`. Its id is 'add_members', which is misleading. It is not restricted to bookings the user may modify (for example, attendee-only views). Seated events are not handled and would get a mix of seat references.

This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

`forEach(async ...)` returns promises that nothing awaits. The `try/catch` around it cannot catch rejections from `getCalendar`, `deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting`. Those rejections become unhandled promise rejections. The function also continues to send emails and return `true` before the calendar and video deletions finish. In a serverless context the work can be cut off. This was already a latent problem, but the PR made the callback async without fixing it. Use `await Promise.all(refs.map(...))` inside the try.

Every entry is `import("./x")` placed directly in an object literal. Each call runs the moment `appStore` is first imported, so all ~29 app packages start loading together. This brings none of the lazy-loading benefit that async imports are supposed to provide. Cold start cost and memory stay the same. A failure in any one app module also becomes an unhandled promise rejection at import time. Entries should be thunks (`() => import(...)`) that are called only when an app is needed.

async forEach callback escapes the try/catch and is not awaited

This is the same issue as in the vital copy. The async `forEach` callbacks are fire-and-forget. Errors are not caught by the surrounding try/catch and become unhandled rejections. The handler returns before the calendar and video deletions complete.
